title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 30
paragraphs: So Solon, having left his native country for that reason and for the sake of seeing the world, came to Amasis in Egypt and also to Croesus at Sardis. There he was entertained as a guest by Croesus in the king's palace; and afterwards, on the third or fourth day, at Croesus's order, the servants led Solon around to see the royal treasuries, and they showed him everything — how great and magnificent it all was. After Solon had looked at it all and examined it at leisure, Croesus asked him, “My Athenian guest, much report of you has come to us, both of your wisdom and of your travels — how, in search of wisdom, you have visited many lands to see them. Now, then, a desire has come upon me to ask whether you have seen any man whom you consider the happiest of all men.” He asked this supposing that he himself was the happiest, but Solon, using no flattery and speaking only the truth, said, “Yes, O king — Tellus the Athenian.” Croesus, astonished at this, asked him earnestly, “In what way do you judge Tellus to be the happiest?” Solon replied, “Tellus, in the first place, lived when his native state was prospering, and he had sons who were fine and good, and saw children born to each of them and all of them growing up. And secondly, he had what with us passes for wealth, and he met with the most glorious end of his life: for when the Athenians fought a battle against their neighbors at Eleusis, he came up in support, routed the enemy, and there died a most noble death. The Athenians buried him publicly on the spot where he fell and honored him greatly.”
